evidenceLabel: Repository-reviewed material; not a claim of production acceptance. Source is pinned, not live-synchronized.

courses.title: Identity, trust & administrator access
courses.description: Understand who the caller is, how Craves verifies access, and why a customer session is not an administrator permission.

lessons.title: From a token to a Craves identity
lessons.overview: Craves attaches an identity to an authenticated request. In the reviewed filter, a Bearer token is passed to CravesJwtService.verifyAccessToken. The resulting claims become CurrentUser: identity ID, Firebase UID, phone number, roles and token version. Think of authentication as checking a staff badge, not opening every door. A valid token identifies the caller; the controller must still decide whether that caller may perform this particular action. This Academy uses the existing verified principal rather than trusting an identity ID sent by the browser.

steps.label: Receive
steps.detail: The backend reads the Authorization header; a missing Bearer token does not create an authenticated principal.

steps.label: Verify
steps.detail: CravesJwtService verifies the access token before claims are accepted.

steps.label: Attach
steps.detail: The filter places CurrentUser and role authorities into the security context.

lessons.example: A customer and an operations administrator may both have valid sessions. Their permitted actions differ because their roles differ.
lessons.lab: In a non-production test, call an Academy endpoint with no token and then with a customer-only principal. Expect 401 and 403 respectively. Never paste a real token into a lesson.
lessons.pitfall: Decoding a JWT payload in the browser is not equivalent to server verification.

questions.prompt: Where should the Academy obtain the learner identity?
options: The visible name in the page header
A userId from the submitted form
A query string supplied by the browser
questions.explanation: The server derives identity from the authenticated principal, preventing progress from being written as someone else.

questions.prompt: Does a valid customer token automatically permit internal Academy access?
options: Yes; if the admin menu is hidden
No; an internal administrator role is also required
Yes; any signed-in user is an administrator
Only when the user changes the URL
questions.explanation: Authentication and authorization are separate checks.

lessons.title: Read the nine internal role boundaries
lessons.overview: InternalAdminRoles defines nine named administrator roles, including PLATFORM_ADMIN, OPERATIONS_ADMIN and AUDIT_ADMIN. These are explicit codes, not an arbitrary string ending in ADMIN. CurrentUser provides case-insensitive role checks. In the Academy, all nine internal roles may learn and read reviewed source. Only platform administrators may change future plans. Platform and audit administrators may read team learning reports. Learners otherwise see their own progress. These Academy permissions do not grant any additional payment, chef or production privileges.

steps.label: Identify
steps.detail: Open InternalAdminRoles and compare each code with its description.

steps.label: Separate
steps.detail: Keep learning access separate from editing plans and viewing other learners.

steps.label: Enforce
steps.detail: Check the verified role on every backend endpoint, not just the navigation link.

lessons.example: A NOTIFICATION_ADMIN can complete a payment lesson without gaining permission to issue refunds.
lessons.lab: Use test principals for each of the nine roles. Verify learning access for all, plan editing only for PLATFORM_ADMIN, and reporting only for PLATFORM_ADMIN or AUDIT_ADMIN.
lessons.pitfall: A role check in a React component improves the interface but is not a security boundary.

questions.prompt: Who may edit Academy future plans?
questions.explanation: The Academy editor checks PLATFORM_ADMIN on the backend.

questions.prompt: Does completing the payment course grant refund access?
options: Only if the course is bookmarked
No; XP never changes production roles
questions.explanation: Learning achievements and production authorization are intentionally independent.

courses.title: Customers, saved addresses & chef onboarding
courses.description: Follow the ownership boundary for customer addresses and the reviewed chef-onboarding workflow.

lessons.title: Browsing location is not an order address
lessons.overview: The User-Chef service owns customer profiles and saved addresses. Its documented recommendation flow compares live GPS coordinates with active saved addresses. A nearby saved address can become SAVED_ADDRESS; otherwise LIVE_GPS supports browsing. The match radius only selects a saved address. It does not quote delivery, approve serviceability, or set a chef delivery area. Checkout must receive an active saved deliveryAddressId owned by the customer. This distinction helps support teams explain why someone can browse meals but still needs to save an address before ordering.

steps.label: Locate
steps.detail: Read live GPS and compare active saved addresses.

steps.label: Recommend
steps.detail: Use SAVED_ADDRESS when it matches; otherwise permit LIVE_GPS browsing.

steps.label: Save
steps.detail: Before checkout, select or create an active saved delivery address.

lessons.example: A customer opens Craves near a new office. Browsing can use GPS immediately, but placing an order requires a saved address with recipient details.
lessons.lab: Using synthetic addresses in a test environment, check the SAVED_ADDRESS and LIVE_GPS recommendation paths. Record expected and actual results without copying real customer coordinates.
lessons.pitfall: matchRadiusMeters is not a delivery pricing or serviceability rule.

questions.prompt: Which location is required for checkout?
options: Any address UUID copied from another user
An active saved address owned by the customer
questions.explanation: Saved-address ownership and active status are validated before checkout.

questions.prompt: What does the saved-address match radius control?
options: Matching GPS to a saved address
questions.explanation: The match radius is a recommendation input, not a delivery policy.

lessons.title: Keep onboarding and operational evidence separate
lessons.overview: The service documentation describes chef applications, KYC document upload, approval or rejection, and notification-outbox workflows. Those are related steps with different evidence. An application being submitted is not the same as a chef being approved. A notification being queued is not proof that an email was delivered. Customer address deletion is documented as soft deletion: the record is no longer available for future orders. For an existing order, use the Order Service snapshot rather than treating an edited profile as historical order data.

steps.label: Review
steps.detail: Check application state and the required supporting documents through authorized admin workflows.

steps.label: Decide
steps.detail: Record an approved decision or rejection using the existing audited operation.

steps.label: Verify
steps.detail: Check downstream notification and catalog state independently; do not assume a queued event means delivery.

lessons.example: An approved chef reports that no message arrived. Investigate the notification request and delivery attempts rather than reapproving the application.
lessons.lab: Draw the application → review → decision → outbox sequence. List one independent piece of evidence for each stage. Do not upload KYC documents into the Academy.
lessons.pitfall: Never use real KYC documents, customer addresses or phone numbers as course examples.

questions.prompt: What proves that an approval email reached the channel provider?
questions.explanation: Submission, approval, enqueueing and channel delivery are separate facts.

questions.prompt: After a saved address is edited, which address should an existing order use?
questions.explanation: Order snapshots preserve the information agreed at checkout.

courses.title: Meal discovery & catalog boundaries
courses.description: Understand nearby meals, query limits, kitchen availability and the difference between browsing and fulfilment.

lessons.title: How nearby discovery finds meals
lessons.overview: The reviewed Catalog documentation describes coordinate-based discovery using PostGIS. The request supplies latitude, longitude and a radius. ST_DWithin filters nearby records and ST_Distance provides nearest-first ordering. The documented public result considers active kitchens and sellable menu items. Pagination bounds the response. The course describes this repository contract, not a guarantee that a particular kitchen is currently open. Runtime availability, later feature changes and production evidence must be checked separately.

steps.label: Validate
steps.detail: Coordinates, a positive radius, and bounded pagination protect the query.

steps.label: Filter
steps.detail: PostGIS applies the requested distance boundary.

steps.label: Return
steps.detail: Nearest-first results include useful kitchen, menu and distance information.

lessons.example: A discovery request with a smaller radius can return fewer kitchens even though the platform has more kitchens overall.
lessons.lab: In a local or staging test, compare the same coordinates with two allowed radii and two pages. Explain changes in count and order using the source contract.
lessons.pitfall: An empty nearby list does not by itself prove that the entire catalog is empty.

questions.prompt: Which documented PostGIS operation filters by radius?
questions.explanation: ST_DWithin applies the spatial distance condition.

questions.prompt: Why does the discovery API bound page size?
options: To protect the response and database workload
questions.explanation: Query limits protect the service and do not define product pricing.

lessons.title: Package metadata travels with the meal
lessons.overview: Catalog records include packaged weight in grams and whether a thermobox is required. These values are relevant to fulfilment, not just the card design. The Order Service copies package metadata during checkout and calculates the chef-specific package. The browsing radius supplied to Catalog does not calculate delivery charges or confirm a provider can fulfil the order. Support should therefore distinguish “the meal is visible” from “this specific order can be delivered under the active policy.”

steps.label: Maintain
steps.detail: The chef maintains the meal and its packaging data through the authorized catalog workflow.

steps.label: Discover
steps.detail: The customer receives discovery data and selects a meal.

steps.label: Snapshot
steps.detail: Checkout copies the relevant metadata into the order boundary.

lessons.example: Two meals from one kitchen can create a heavier combined package than either meal alone. The final delivery decision must use order-level facts.
lessons.lab: Trace packaged weight and thermobox fields from a test menu response to the checkout snapshot. Confirm units explicitly; do not assume kilograms.
lessons.pitfall: Never turn a browsing radius into an undocumented permanent chef delivery limit.

questions.prompt: What unit is explicitly documented for packaged menu weight?
questions.explanation: Catalog documents packaged weight in grams.

questions.prompt: Does appearing in nearby discovery confirm final delivery serviceability?
options: No; discovery and delivery checks are separate
Yes, when the card has an image
questions.explanation: The catalog browsing radius is not a delivery serviceability policy.

courses.title: Checkout, snapshots & chef-specific orders
courses.description: Trace multi-kitchen checkout, saved-address validation and the fulfilment information that must not drift.

lessons.title: One checkout, one order per kitchen
lessons.overview: The Order Service owns carts and checkout. The reviewed contract groups cart items by kitchen, writes one parent checkout, and creates one chef-specific order for each kitchen. It validates the customer’s saved address using the User-Chef internal API and refreshes active menu and kitchen data from Catalog. The documented write is transactional. This gives operations a precise way to reason about a multi-kitchen purchase: one customer checkout can have several independently fulfilled kitchen orders.

steps.label: Resolve
steps.detail: Read the customer identity from the verified request and validate the owned saved address.

steps.label: Refresh
steps.detail: Resolve current active menu and kitchen records from their owning service.

steps.label: Create
steps.detail: Persist the parent checkout and the chef-specific orders in the transaction.

lessons.example: A cart contains meals from Kitchen A and Kitchen B. Expect one checkout and two kitchen orders, not one rider assignment inferred from the cart alone.
lessons.lab: Create a synthetic two-kitchen cart in a safe test environment. Verify parent-child references, ownership validation and rollback if a required lookup fails.
lessons.pitfall: Do not accept a customer identity ID from a form as proof of saved-address ownership.

questions.prompt: A checkout contains meals from two kitchens. What is the documented order structure?
options: One kitchen record overwritten by the other
One order with no kitchen boundary
One parent checkout and two kitchen-specific orders
questions.explanation: Checkout groups items by kitchen and creates one order for each kitchen.

questions.prompt: Which service is the source of truth for the saved customer address?
questions.explanation: Order validates the saved address against User-Chef before storing its snapshot.

lessons.title: Why historical order information is immutable
lessons.overview: Order stores customer drop-off and kitchen pickup snapshots, alongside item and package information. These snapshots preserve what was agreed at checkout when the underlying profile or kitchen changes later. The reviewed documentation also states that chef acceptance persists ready_at from preparation time. A ready time is a scheduling input, not proof that a rider has accepted. Separate checkout, payment, chef acceptance, readiness and delivery evidence when investigating an order.

steps.label: Capture
steps.detail: Copy the relevant pickup, drop-off and package data at checkout.

steps.label: Accept
steps.detail: Chef acceptance records preparation time and ready_at.

steps.label: Investigate
steps.detail: Follow the kitchen-specific order and its state history rather than reconstructing history from current profiles.

lessons.example: A customer edits their saved address after payment. The already-created order must still show its checkout drop-off snapshot.
lessons.lab: In a non-production test, create an order, edit the source address, and confirm the order snapshot remains unchanged. Capture only synthetic data.
lessons.pitfall: A healthy service revision or successful payment does not prove that every fulfilment step is complete.

questions.prompt: Which data should delivery execution use for an existing order?
options: The most recently edited profile values
Any GPS value currently in the browser
The first address returned by search
The stored order pickup and drop-off snapshots
questions.explanation: Snapshots preserve historical checkout facts.

questions.prompt: What does ready_at represent in the reviewed order flow?
options: A preparation-based scheduling time persisted on chef acceptance
questions.explanation: Chef acceptance and preparation time establish ready_at; delivery has its own evidence.

courses.title: Payments: verification before fulfilment
courses.description: Read the current Razorpay-aware payment service and learn why a browser success callback is not the final authority.

lessons.title: Create payment from an owned checkout
lessons.overview: PaymentService first fetches an owned checkout and checks the checkout ID, total and customer identity. It can reuse a compatible existing payment order rather than create a duplicate blindly. The reviewed implementation supports a Razorpay verification branch and retains other provider code; source presence alone does not identify the currently enabled production provider. The amount and currency come from server-owned checkout facts, not a price edited in the browser.

steps.label: Authorize
steps.detail: Fetch the checkout using the authenticated customer context.

steps.label: Validate
steps.detail: Require the checkout identity, customer and total needed for payment.

steps.label: Reuse or create
steps.detail: Check a compatible existing payment order before calling the configured provider.

lessons.example: A user refreshes the payment screen after a slow response. Diagnose the existing checkout/payment relationship before creating another external order.
lessons.lab: Use mocked providers or a sandbox to test repeat create requests and cross-customer access. Do not make live payments for course exercises.
lessons.pitfall: A provider implementation in Git is not evidence that the provider is production-enabled.

questions.prompt: Where should the payable amount come from?
options: A value edited in browser developer tools
questions.explanation: PaymentService uses the owned checkout and validates required totals.

questions.prompt: How should a retry be investigated?
options: Always create a new provider order
Assume payment failed because the page refreshed
Check the existing payment-order relationship before recreating
questions.explanation: The reviewed create flow can reuse an existing compatible payment order.

lessons.title: Verify payment and handle repeated signals
lessons.overview: The Razorpay branch verifies the provider order, payment ID, signature, expected amount and currency through RazorpayPaymentClient. PaymentService updates a payment to PAID only through the verified path. The reviewed SQL update includes a status guard and notifies Order when a new transition is recorded. Webhook handling checks the provider signature. A front-end success animation, a webhook arrival, and a verified paid transition are different pieces of evidence. Teach those distinctions before investigating money or triggering fulfilment.

steps.label: Match
steps.detail: Match provider identifiers to the stored Craves payment order.

steps.label: Verify
steps.detail: Check the signature and expected money through the provider verification path.

steps.label: Transition
steps.detail: Record the paid transition and notify the order side only when the transition is new.

lessons.example: The browser callback and provider webhook both arrive. The system must not grant two paid transitions or create two delivery jobs.
lessons.lab: With a mocked provider, test valid and invalid signatures plus duplicate payment signals. Confirm that no unverified payload changes the order to paid.
lessons.pitfall: Never paste live API keys, webhook secrets, real payment payloads or customer details into course notes.

questions.prompt: Is the browser success callback alone enough to mark a Craves order paid?
options: No; the server must verify payment details
Only when the browser is Chrome
Yes; if a screenshot is attached
questions.explanation: Server verification protects the payment transition.

questions.prompt: Why guard the PAID status update?
options: To avoid repeating a state transition when signals are duplicated
To hide failed payments from support
To let the browser choose the status
questions.explanation: The transition guard makes repeated verified signals distinguishable from a new paid transition.

courses.title: Delivery timing, ranking & provider evidence
courses.description: Understand the Craves delivery boundary: chef readiness, provider capabilities, ranking and durable duplicate protection.

lessons.title: Payment is not the delivery-create trigger
lessons.overview: The documented Craves delivery rule is explicit: payment success must not immediately create a delivery. The Order Service first records chef acceptance and preparation time, and scheduling happens close to the calculated ready time. The final job is associated with a chef-specific sub-order. This reduces incorrect assumptions about multi-kitchen checkouts. Every claim that a provider is active must be based on its real production configuration and successful runtime evidence, not a green build or a registry row alone.

steps.label: Wait for acceptance
steps.detail: Use the kitchen order’s chef-acceptance and preparation facts.

steps.label: Schedule near readiness
steps.detail: Use the calculated ready time instead of dispatching immediately on payment.

steps.label: Verify the provider job
steps.detail: Check the real create response and provider job identifier; do not invent a rider.

lessons.example: Two kitchens accept at different times. Their sub-orders can have different preparation and delivery timelines even though the customer paid once.
lessons.lab: Trace a synthetic order through payment, chef acceptance, ready_at and delivery scheduling using mocks. Verify that payment alone never creates a job.
lessons.pitfall: Provider registration, successful CI and a real accepted delivery job are three different facts.

questions.prompt: Which event must not immediately create a delivery by itself?
questions.explanation: The documented timing rule waits for chef acceptance and preparation-based readiness.

questions.prompt: What is the final delivery-job boundary?
questions.explanation: Each chef-specific sub-order has its own fulfilment boundary.

lessons.title: Rank real candidates; preserve the decision
lessons.overview: The reviewed delivery design combines provider quality with proximity or ETA and persists assignment decisions. It documents a seven-day live score window, historical fade, and Thompson-sampling state. These describe the repository design, not a calibrated claim about real-world prediction accuracy. For an adapter that exposes quotes but not nearby riders, the candidates are provider quotes. The engine must not fabricate rider locations. Assignment is documented as idempotent by chefSubOrderId, and terminal outcome receipts prevent duplicate scoring updates.

steps.label: Check capability
steps.detail: Determine whether the actual adapter returns quotes or genuine rider candidates.

steps.label: Rank
steps.detail: Apply the configured scoring strategy to available, real candidates.

steps.label: Persist
steps.detail: Reuse the recorded assignment on retries and deduplicate terminal outcome updates.

lessons.example: A repeated assignment request returns its existing decision instead of rerandomizing and accidentally creating a second provider job.
lessons.lab: With synthetic candidates, submit the same sub-order twice and confirm the selected decision is stable. Submit a terminal outcome twice and check for one scoring update.
lessons.pitfall: Adaptive scoring and configured priors are not proof of a model trained or calibrated on production outcomes.

questions.prompt: An adapter exposes quotes but no rider coordinates. What should Craves rank?
options: A list generated from chef names
questions.explanation: The engine must respect the adapter’s genuine capabilities.

questions.prompt: What should a retry of an existing assignment do?
options: Create a different provider job immediately
questions.explanation: The documented idempotency boundary is chefSubOrderId.

courses.title: Subscription foundations & policy ownership
courses.description: Separate plans, customer subscription state and approved business policy without inventing commercial rules.

lessons.title: A plan is not a customer subscription
lessons.overview: The Subscription Service documentation distinguishes subscription plans from customer subscription records and lifecycle tracking. It has separate customer and admin routes, validates Craves JWTs and owns subscription_schema in the business database. A plan describes an offering; a customer subscription records a particular customer’s participation and current lifecycle state. Inspect current code and configured policies before making claims about schedules, pauses or renewals, because foundational documentation is not a complete production acceptance record.

steps.label: Read the plan
steps.detail: Identify the offering and its allowed state through the plan API.

steps.label: Read participation
steps.detail: Identify the customer-owned subscription record.

steps.label: Check lifecycle
steps.detail: Use the relevant validated lifecycle operation rather than treating a plan edit as a customer-state change.

lessons.example: Pausing one customer’s subscription should not be explained as disabling the entire subscription plan.
lessons.lab: Using synthetic records, identify one plan and two customer subscriptions. Explain which IDs and state changes belong to which object.
lessons.pitfall: The existence of a pause endpoint does not define every commercial cutoff or refund rule.

questions.prompt: What does a customer subscription record represent?
options: A specific customer’s participation and lifecycle
questions.explanation: Plans and individual customer subscriptions are different domain objects.

questions.prompt: Does a foundational README prove production acceptance?
options: Yes, if the module name is correct
No; check current configuration and runtime evidence
Yes, if it includes an endpoint
Only if it has a logo
questions.explanation: Repository descriptions are not a substitute for deployment and acceptance evidence.

lessons.title: Do not invent financial or meal-credit rules
lessons.overview: The foundation documentation explicitly reserves several business decisions for Product, Finance and Operations, including pricing strategy, unused credits, payout calculation, holidays, cancellation cutoffs and renewal mandates. Later implementation may add approved policy; verify it in the current source and runtime settings. The Academy future-plans area therefore labels proposals separately from approved or shipped work. A proposed idea must never be taught as an active customer entitlement or as an instruction to alter real charges.

steps.label: Locate policy
steps.detail: Find the approved rule and the current implementation or configuration.

steps.label: Label uncertainty
steps.detail: Distinguish a proposal from an approved decision and a deployed behavior.

steps.label: Escalate safely
steps.detail: Route missing commercial decisions to the authorized business owner.

lessons.example: A support question asks whether unused meals roll over. Check the approved live policy instead of answering from a plausible assumption.
lessons.lab: Write a synthetic policy question and identify the approval and implementation evidence needed to answer it. Do not edit a real subscription for training.
lessons.pitfall: Course XP and quiz results must never trigger customer charges, refunds, credits or payouts.

questions.prompt: What should a learner do when a commercial rule is not established by the evidence?
options: Check with the authorized policy owner
questions.explanation: Policy uncertainty should be made explicit and resolved through the authorized owner.

questions.prompt: How should an unapproved future idea be shown?
options: As PROPOSED, separate from implemented behavior
questions.explanation: The private roadmap uses explicit lifecycle labels to avoid confusing plans with facts.

courses.title: Notification requests, delivery & recovery
courses.description: Learn the difference between an inbox record, a queued request and verified delivery through a configured channel.

lessons.title: Know what a notification record proves
lessons.overview: The Notification Service owns in-app inbox records, notification request audit information, channel delivery attempts and templates. Its foundation documentation distinguishes persisted in-app notifications from email, SMS or push requests that need enabled provider adapters. Do not interpret those historical defaults as a statement that every current external channel is disabled. Investigate the specific channel’s current configuration and delivery evidence. Phone OTP belongs to Firebase Authentication and Craves Auth, not this transactional-notification boundary.

steps.label: Identify the event
steps.detail: Find the relevant Craves event and requested channel.

steps.label: Inspect state
steps.detail: Distinguish a recorded request from a successful channel delivery.

steps.label: Check ownership
steps.detail: Route phone-OTP issues to the Auth boundary instead of the notification inbox.

lessons.example: A chef sees an in-app message but not an email. The in-app success does not prove the email provider accepted the corresponding request.
lessons.lab: With a mock notification request, record the request state and channel-attempt state separately. Do not send real SMS or email from an Academy exercise.
lessons.pitfall: Never use a queued record as proof that a customer received a message.

questions.prompt: Where does the documented phone-OTP responsibility belong?
questions.explanation: OTP and transactional notifications are different service responsibilities.

questions.prompt: What does a persisted notification request prove by itself?
options: That the chef approved an order
questions.explanation: Delivery and reading require their own evidence.

lessons.title: Recover without exposing customer data
lessons.overview: The documented internal create route uses service authentication and records a request key. Recovery must preserve the relationship between the source event, recipient, channel and attempts. Investigate the current failure before retrying; a replay without context can create confusing duplicate messages. Training should use synthetic recipients and provider mocks. The Academy does not collect phone numbers, email bodies, notification payloads or browser keystrokes as learning telemetry.

steps.label: Trace
steps.detail: Follow the original request key, source service and event.

steps.label: Diagnose
steps.detail: Check the current provider configuration and attempt result.

steps.label: Retry safely
steps.detail: Use the approved recovery path and verify its outcome instead of blindly resending.

lessons.example: A delivery provider outage delayed an email. Record the original event and recovery attempt as separate evidence rather than changing the event history.
lessons.lab: Build a paper recovery checklist using a fake request key and recipient. Include authorization, duplicate checks, expected result and evidence to retain.
lessons.pitfall: Internal service keys and real customer message bodies must not enter the Academy source examples or telemetry.

questions.prompt: What is the safest first step before recovery?
options: Trace the original event and inspect its current failure
Paste the service key into chat
Assume every pending request failed permanently
questions.explanation: Investigation comes before an authorized recovery action.

questions.prompt: Which information should Academy telemetry avoid?
options: Real message bodies and customer contact details
questions.explanation: Learning telemetry does not require customer or message-content data.

courses.title: Web BFF, source literacy & release evidence
courses.description: Understand the thin Next.js proxy boundary and how to tell source existence, build success and production acceptance apart.

lessons.title: The browser talks through a controlled boundary
lessons.overview: The reviewed server-api helper reads the Craves access-token cookie on the server and forwards a Bearer token to a configured HTTPS API base URL. It rejects unsafe paths, uses no-store caching and aborts requests after a timeout. The admin identity route calls /auth/me and checks adminEnabled. The Academy follows that boundary: its Next.js route is a controlled proxy, while grading, XP and persistence remain in Java. A new learning feature is not a reason to extend the legacy Node backend.

steps.label: Receive
steps.detail: The browser calls a same-origin Academy route using its existing session.

steps.label: Constrain
steps.detail: The BFF allowlists actions, checks mutation origin and enforces body limits.

steps.label: Authorize again
steps.detail: The Java endpoint checks the verified administrator role and owns the actual learning operation.

lessons.example: A user edits a browser request to add somebody else’s identity ID. The backend ignores client identity claims and uses CurrentUser.
lessons.lab: Test missing cookies, cross-origin mutation requests, unknown routes and unavailable upstream behavior. Verify fail-closed responses and no source leakage.
lessons.pitfall: Do not put quiz answers, internal service secrets or the complete curriculum into a public JavaScript bundle.

questions.prompt: Where does Academy grading and XP persistence belong?
questions.explanation: The BFF remains thin; the backend is authoritative for learning state.

questions.prompt: What should happen when upstream identity verification is unavailable?
options: Give the user a new production role
Fail closed and show an actionable error
Assume the user is an administrator
questions.explanation: Unavailable verification must not become a permission bypass.

lessons.title: Read evidence before declaring a feature live
lessons.overview: A file in the repository proves that source exists at a particular revision. A passing build proves that selected checks completed. Neither alone proves that the new image is deployed, the database migration applied, the APIM route exists, the feature is enabled, or an authenticated smoke test passed. The Academy pins its course-source revision and labels its material as repository-based. Future plans are maintained separately in private runtime storage, and a human must confirm the evidence before teaching a changed behavior as live.

steps.label: Pin source
steps.detail: Record the commit used for a course or release assessment.

steps.label: Check build and deployment
steps.detail: Identify the tested artifact, healthy deployed revision, migration and route configuration.

steps.label: Validate behavior
steps.detail: Run authorized positive and negative smoke tests and retain the results.

lessons.example: A new Academy page compiles but APIM returns 404. The page is implemented; the full feature is not production-accepted yet.
lessons.lab: Create a release checklist with source SHA, CI result, image tag, revision, migration, API route, admin smoke test, customer-denial test and rollback action.
lessons.pitfall: Do not treat a planned status, a generated video script or a screenshot as runtime proof.

questions.prompt: Does a successful build alone prove the Academy is live?
options: Yes, if the UI looks polished
No; deployment, routing, migration and authenticated validation are also needed
Only if the branch is named main
questions.explanation: Build and production acceptance are different evidence stages.

questions.prompt: What should a course display to make its source traceable?
options: The pinned source revision and reviewed file references
questions.explanation: Provenance makes the lesson’s source boundary explicit.
